## Eligibility

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Eligibility")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/14_September_2012_-_Olympians_and_Paralympians_-_14_Medi_2012_-_Olympaidd_a_Pharalympaidd_%288008934725%29.jpg/250px-14_September_2012_-_Olympians_and_Paralympians_-_14_Medi_2012_-_Olympaidd_a_Pharalympaidd_%288008934725%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:14_September_2012_-_Olympians_and_Paralympians_-_14_Medi_2012_-_Olympaidd_a_Pharalympaidd_(8008934725).jpg)

A heroes' welcome for Welsh Olympians and Paralympians at the [Senedd building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senedd_building "Senedd building"), 2012

As the [National Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Olympic_Committee "National Olympic Committee") (NOC) for the United Kingdom, the [British Olympic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Olympic_Association "British Olympic Association") (BOA) membership encompasses the four [Home Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Nations "Home Nations") of the United Kingdom ([England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"), [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland"), [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") and [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales "Wales"), who notably compete separately in many international sports outside Olympic competition for historic reasons), plus the three [Crown Dependencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Dependencies "Crown Dependencies") ([Guernsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bailiwick_of_Guernsey "Bailiwick of Guernsey"), [Isle of Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Man "Isle of Man") and [Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey "Jersey")), and all but three of the [British Overseas Territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Overseas_Territories "British Overseas Territories")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-3)([Bermuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda_at_the_Olympics "Bermuda at the Olympics"), [British Virgin Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Virgin_Islands_at_the_Olympics "British Virgin Islands at the Olympics") and [Cayman Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayman_Islands_at_the_Olympics "Cayman Islands at the Olympics") have their own NOCs).

Representatives of the [devolved Northern Ireland government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Executive "Northern Ireland Executive") and others in the region have objected to the name "Team GB" as discriminatory and called for it to be renamed as "Team UK" to make it clearer that Northern Ireland is included on the team.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-5)

Under the IOC charter, the [Olympic Federation of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Federation_of_Ireland "Olympic Federation of Ireland") is also responsible for the entire island of [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-6) However, athletes from [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland") can elect to represent either Great Britain or [Ireland at the Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland_at_the_Olympics "Ireland at the Olympics"), as [people of Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_of_Northern_Ireland "People of Northern Ireland"). A number of Northern Irish-born athletes, particularly in boxing, have won medals for Ireland at the Games, while a small number of athletes from Northern Ireland have represented both Team GB and Team Ireland, most recently swimming gold medallist [Jack McMillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_McMillan_(swimmer) "Jack McMillan (swimmer)").

Usually most of Northern Ireland's athletes at the Olympics compete for Team Ireland. At the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics"), 6 athletes (16%) from Northern Ireland, represented Great Britain, while 31 athletes (84%) represented Ireland.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-7) In 2016, eight represented Great Britain and 21 represented Ireland.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-8)

All athletes from the whole of [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland") were included in the Great Britain team up until the 1920 Olympics as the entire island was part of the United Kingdom at that time. Hence the Team GB claim to have won at least one gold at every Summer Games is partially founded on a single Irish athlete, [Tom Kiely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Kiely "Tom Kiely"), who won gold in the [1904 St. Louis games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_St._Louis_Games "1904 St. Louis Games"). While Kiely himself objected to the designation, considering himself simply Irish, Olympic historians recognise his medal as won by Great Britain and Ireland, thus maintaining the unique British record.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-9)

The existence of a Great Britain team has been criticised by [Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_nationalism "Welsh nationalism") and [Scottish nationalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_nationalists "Scottish nationalists"), advocating for separate [Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_in_Wales#Calls_for_Wales_Olympic_team "Sport in Wales")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:0-10) and [Scottish Olympic teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_for_a_Scottish_Olympic_Team "Campaign for a Scottish Olympic Team") instead.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-13)

Other nations that formed part of the then [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire"), however, were represented separately even before full independence in a variety of ways, either as fledgling nations such as [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa_at_the_Olympics "South Africa at the Olympics") and [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_at_the_Olympics "India at the Olympics"), or occasionally in regional teams such as [Australasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australasia_at_the_Olympics "Australasia at the Olympics") and British [West Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_West_Indies_at_the_1960_Summer_Olympics "British West Indies at the 1960 Summer Olympics").

## Hosted games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Hosted games")]

The United Kingdom has hosted the Summer Games on three occasions – 1908, 1948 and 2012, all in London – second only to the United States. At the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics") in Rio, [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Great Britain at the 2016 Summer Olympics") became the first team to win more medals at a Summer Olympics immediately after hosting a Summer Olympics; they won 67 medals overall, coming in second place in the medal table ahead of [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "China at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), two more than in [London in 2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics"). This success came 20 years after finishing 36th in the medal table, after winning just one gold and fourteen other medals at the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics") in Atlanta, which led to significant changes in the management and funding of British sports and facilities.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-14)

[London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") also won the right to host the 1944 Summer Olympics. However, the 1944 games were cancelled due to the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War").

### Potential future bids

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Potential future bids")]

In February 2019, the [Mayor of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London "Mayor of London")[Sadiq Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadiq_Khan "Sadiq Khan") announced plans to bid for the [2032](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2032_Summer_Olympics "2032 Summer Olympics") or 2036 Olympics, which was backed by [UK Sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Sport "UK Sport").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-15) However, it has been speculated that either [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester") or [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham") may be in the frame to host future games, rather than London. In July 2021, the 2032 Games were awarded to [Brisbane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane "Brisbane").

In July 2024, Khan revealed he was to attend the opening ceremony of the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics") in Paris and would use the opportunity to lobby members of the British Olympic Association and the [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom") (a potential bid would need to be both underwritten by the government and backed by the BOA) into hosting the 2040 Olympics.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-16) He claimed London could host the "greenest games ever" by reusing venues from the 2012 games including the London Stadium, the London Aquatics Centre, Lee Valley Velopark and Copper Box Arena. The idea was backed by [Tom Daley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Daley "Tom Daley"), Team GB diver, commenting that "London is one of the few cities on the planet where you would be able to host the games tomorrow".

A 2025 proposal by the Heseltine Institute would see Manchester and [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool "Liverpool") launch a joint bid for the 2040 Games - this idea was backed by the Mayor of Greater Manchester [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham"), who described the prospect of the two cities hosting the games as an opportunity to 'rebalance the country'.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-17)

Notes
*   **NAT**Australian [Frederick Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Lane "Frederick Lane") competed at the [1900 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Summer_Olympics "1900 Summer Olympics"), winning two gold medals in the [swimming events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "Swimming at the 1900 Summer Olympics"). As a representative of a British club, his participation and medals were attributed accordingly.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-22)Conversely, British [Lloyd Hildebrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd_Hildebrand "Lloyd Hildebrand") won a silver medal in the [25 km cycling event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_25_kilometres "Cycling at the 1900 Summer Olympics – Men's 25 kilometres"). As a representative of a French club, his participation and medal were attributed to France.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-23)
*   **MIX**At the 1900 Summer Olympics [four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Summer_Olympics_medal_table#Team_events "1900 Summer Olympics medal table") team event medals (3 gold and 1 silver) won by British clubs competing as [mixed teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_teams_at_the_Olympics "Mixed teams at the Olympics")—composed primarily of British athletes alongside a few non-British participants—were attributed to Great Britain: gold in the [5000 metres team race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_5000_metres_team_race "Athletics at the 1900 Summer Olympics – Men's 5000 metres team race"), [polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polo_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "Polo at the 1900 Summer Olympics"), and [water polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_polo_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "Water polo at the 1900 Summer Olympics") and silver in polo.
*   **ART**[Art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the Summer Olympics") (1912–1948) are not included in the medal table above, as they were [non-sports events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_sports#Feats_and_artistic_events "Olympic sports") formerly part of the Olympic Games.[[nb 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-art-24)Great Britain won a total of nine art competition medals (3 gold, 5 silver and 1 bronze), across the [1920](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1920_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1920 Summer Olympics"), [1924](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1924_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1924 Summer Olympics"), [1928](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1928_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1928 Summer Olympics"), [1932](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1932_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1932 Summer Olympics") and [1948 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1948_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1948 Summer Olympics").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-olympics_gbr-19)

The [United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Northern_Ireland "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland"), referred to as simply "Great Britain", has been represented at every modern [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games"). As of the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics"), it is third in the [all-time Summer Olympic medal table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-time_Olympic_Games_medal_table "All-time Olympic Games medal table") by overall number of medals and fourth in number of gold medals won. London hosted the [Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games") in [1908](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_Summer_Olympics "1908 Summer Olympics"), [1948](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_Summer_Olympics "1948 Summer Olympics") and [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics").

Athletes from the United Kingdom compete as part of the Great Britain and Northern Ireland Olympic Team,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-1) branded "[Team GB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_GB "Team GB")". The team is organised by the [British Olympic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Olympic_Association "British Olympic Association"), the [National Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Olympic_Committee "National Olympic Committee") for the UK. Team GB also represents the three [Crown Dependencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Dependencies "Crown Dependencies") of [Guernsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernsey "Guernsey"), [Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey "Jersey") and the [Isle of Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Man "Isle of Man") and the UK's [Overseas Territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Overseas_Territories "British Overseas Territories") (with the exceptions of [Bermuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda_at_the_Olympics "Bermuda at the Olympics"), the [British Virgin Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Virgin_Islands_at_the_Olympics "British Virgin Islands at the Olympics") and the [Cayman Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayman_Islands_at_the_Olympics "Cayman Islands at the Olympics")). Athletes from [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland") can choose to compete for either Great Britain or [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland_at_the_Olympics "Ireland at the Olympics"), with most choosing Ireland.[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-2) The use of "Great Britain" over "United Kingdom" has faced criticism in Northern Ireland.

British athletes have won a combined total of 1,025 medals at the Olympic Games; 979 of those medals were won at the Summer Olympics, where Team GB is the only team to have won at least one gold medal at every games. Team GB is also the only team to have won at least one athletics medal at every Summer Olympic Games. The team has been less successful at the Winter Olympics, winning 39 medals, 15 of them gold. The UK finished in first place on the medals table at the 1908 games, placed second at the 2016 games and third at the [1900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Summer_Olympics "1900 Summer Olympics"), [1912](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1912_Summer_Olympics "1912 Summer Olympics"), [1920](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1920_Summer_Olympics "1920 Summer Olympics") and 2012 games.

The most successful British Olympian by gold medals and total medals won is [Sir Jason Kenny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Kenny "Jason Kenny"), who has won seven gold medals and nine overall, all in track cycling. The cyclist [Dame Laura Kenny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Kenny "Laura Kenny") and the dressage rider [Charlotte Dujardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Dujardin "Charlotte Dujardin") share the record for the most medals won by a female British athlete, with six each; Kenny's five gold medals are the female British record. The most successful Winter Olympians from Team GB are skeleton racers [Lizzy Yarnold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lizzy_Yarnold "Lizzy Yarnold") and [Matt Weston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Weston_(skeleton_racer) "Matt Weston (skeleton racer)"), with two gold medals each.

As the [National Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Olympic_Committee "National Olympic Committee") (NOC) for the United Kingdom, the [British Olympic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Olympic_Association "British Olympic Association") (BOA) membership encompasses the four [Home Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Nations "Home Nations") of the United Kingdom ([England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"), [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland"), [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") and [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales "Wales"), who notably compete separately in many international sports outside Olympic competition for historic reasons), plus the three [Crown Dependencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Dependencies "Crown Dependencies") ([Guernsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bailiwick_of_Guernsey "Bailiwick of Guernsey"), [Isle of Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Man "Isle of Man") and [Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey "Jersey")), and all but three of the [British Overseas Territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Overseas_Territories "British Overseas Territories")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-3)([Bermuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda_at_the_Olympics "Bermuda at the Olympics"), [British Virgin Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Virgin_Islands_at_the_Olympics "British Virgin Islands at the Olympics") and [Cayman Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayman_Islands_at_the_Olympics "Cayman Islands at the Olympics") have their own NOCs).

Representatives of the [devolved Northern Ireland government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Executive "Northern Ireland Executive") and others in the region have objected to the name "Team GB" as discriminatory and called for it to be renamed as "Team UK" to make it clearer that Northern Ireland is included on the team.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-5)

Under the IOC charter, the [Olympic Federation of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Federation_of_Ireland "Olympic Federation of Ireland") is also responsible for the entire island of [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-6) However, athletes from [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland") can elect to represent either Great Britain or [Ireland at the Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland_at_the_Olympics "Ireland at the Olympics"), as [people of Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_of_Northern_Ireland "People of Northern Ireland"). A number of Northern Irish-born athletes, particularly in boxing, have won medals for Ireland at the Games, while a small number of athletes from Northern Ireland have represented both Team GB and Team Ireland, most recently swimming gold medallist [Jack McMillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_McMillan_(swimmer) "Jack McMillan (swimmer)").

Usually most of Northern Ireland's athletes at the Olympics compete for Team Ireland. At the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics"), 6 athletes (16%) from Northern Ireland, represented Great Britain, while 31 athletes (84%) represented Ireland.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-7) In 2016, eight represented Great Britain and 21 represented Ireland.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-8)

All athletes from the whole of [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland") were included in the Great Britain team up until the 1920 Olympics as the entire island was part of the United Kingdom at that time. Hence the Team GB claim to have won at least one gold at every Summer Games is partially founded on a single Irish athlete, [Tom Kiely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Kiely "Tom Kiely"), who won gold in the [1904 St. Louis games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_St._Louis_Games "1904 St. Louis Games"). While Kiely himself objected to the designation, considering himself simply Irish, Olympic historians recognise his medal as won by Great Britain and Ireland, thus maintaining the unique British record.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-9)

The existence of a Great Britain team has been criticised by [Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_nationalism "Welsh nationalism") and [Scottish nationalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_nationalists "Scottish nationalists"), advocating for separate [Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_in_Wales#Calls_for_Wales_Olympic_team "Sport in Wales")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:0-10) and [Scottish Olympic teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_for_a_Scottish_Olympic_Team "Campaign for a Scottish Olympic Team") instead.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-13)

Other nations that formed part of the then [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire"), however, were represented separately even before full independence in a variety of ways, either as fledgling nations such as [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa_at_the_Olympics "South Africa at the Olympics") and [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_at_the_Olympics "India at the Olympics"), or occasionally in regional teams such as [Australasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australasia_at_the_Olympics "Australasia at the Olympics") and British [West Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_West_Indies_at_the_1960_Summer_Olympics "British West Indies at the 1960 Summer Olympics").

## Hosted games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Hosted games")]

The United Kingdom has hosted the Summer Games on three occasions – 1908, 1948 and 2012, all in London – second only to the United States. At the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics") in Rio, [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Great Britain at the 2016 Summer Olympics") became the first team to win more medals at a Summer Olympics immediately after hosting a Summer Olympics; they won 67 medals overall, coming in second place in the medal table ahead of [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "China at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), two more than in [London in 2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics"). This success came 20 years after finishing 36th in the medal table, after winning just one gold and fourteen other medals at the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics") in Atlanta, which led to significant changes in the management and funding of British sports and facilities.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-14)

[London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") also won the right to host the 1944 Summer Olympics. However, the 1944 games were cancelled due to the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War").

### Potential future bids

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Potential future bids")]

In February 2019, the [Mayor of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London "Mayor of London")[Sadiq Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadiq_Khan "Sadiq Khan") announced plans to bid for the [2032](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2032_Summer_Olympics "2032 Summer Olympics") or 2036 Olympics, which was backed by [UK Sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Sport "UK Sport").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-15) However, it has been speculated that either [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester") or [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham") may be in the frame to host future games, rather than London. In July 2021, the 2032 Games were awarded to [Brisbane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane "Brisbane").

In July 2024, Khan revealed he was to attend the opening ceremony of the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics") in Paris and would use the opportunity to lobby members of the British Olympic Association and the [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom") (a potential bid would need to be both underwritten by the government and backed by the BOA) into hosting the 2040 Olympics.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-16) He claimed London could host the "greenest games ever" by reusing venues from the 2012 games including the London Stadium, the London Aquatics Centre, Lee Valley Velopark and Copper Box Arena. The idea was backed by [Tom Daley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Daley "Tom Daley"), Team GB diver, commenting that "London is one of the few cities on the planet where you would be able to host the games tomorrow".

A 2025 proposal by the Heseltine Institute would see Manchester and [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool "Liverpool") launch a joint bid for the 2040 Games - this idea was backed by the Mayor of Greater Manchester [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham"), who described the prospect of the two cities hosting the games as an opportunity to 'rebalance the country'.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-17)

Notes
*   **NAT**Australian [Frederick Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Lane "Frederick Lane") competed at the [1900 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Summer_Olympics "1900 Summer Olympics"), winning two gold medals in the [swimming events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "Swimming at the 1900 Summer Olympics"). As a representative of a British club, his participation and medals were attributed accordingly.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-22)Conversely, British [Lloyd Hildebrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd_Hildebrand "Lloyd Hildebrand") won a silver medal in the [25 km cycling event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_25_kilometres "Cycling at the 1900 Summer Olympics – Men's 25 kilometres"). As a representative of a French club, his participation and medal were attributed to France.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-23)
*   **MIX**At the 1900 Summer Olympics [four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Summer_Olympics_medal_table#Team_events "1900 Summer Olympics medal table") team event medals (3 gold and 1 silver) won by British clubs competing as [mixed teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_teams_at_the_Olympics "Mixed teams at the Olympics")—composed primarily of British athletes alongside a few non-British participants—were attributed to Great Britain: gold in the [5000 metres team race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_5000_metres_team_race "Athletics at the 1900 Summer Olympics – Men's 5000 metres team race"), [polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polo_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "Polo at the 1900 Summer Olympics"), and [water polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_polo_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "Water polo at the 1900 Summer Olympics") and silver in polo.
*   **ART**[Art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the Summer Olympics") (1912–1948) are not included in the medal table above, as they were [non-sports events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_sports#Feats_and_artistic_events "Olympic sports") formerly part of the Olympic Games.[[nb 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-art-24)Great Britain won a total of nine art competition medals (3 gold, 5 silver and 1 bronze), across the [1920](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1920_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1920 Summer Olympics"), [1924](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1924_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1924 Summer Olympics"), [1928](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1928_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1928 Summer Olympics"), [1932](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1932_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1932 Summer Olympics") and [1948 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1948_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1948 Summer Olympics").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-olympics_gbr-19)

[Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") first participated at the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") in 1912, and has competed at almost every Games since then. The nation was not invited to the 1948 Games after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), and was part of the [American-led boycott of the 1980 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American-led_boycott_of_the_1980_Summer_Olympics "American-led boycott of the 1980 Summer Olympics") in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow").

Since its first (ultimately canceled) bid in 1940, Japan has hosted the Olympics four times: in 1964, 1972, 1998, and 2021 (originally 2020). Each occasion coincided with critical turning points in Japan's domestic development or global standing. The [1964 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Summer_Olympics "1964 Summer Olympics") were a pivotal moment in Japan's postwar recovery, offering a visual spectacle of modernization that included the unveiling of the [Shinkansen bullet train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinkansen "Shinkansen") and the rapid reconstruction of Tokyo's infrastructure. The event symbolized Japan's reintegration into the international community after its defeat in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_in_WWII "Japan in WWII"), marking its transition from a militaristic empire to a peaceful economic power aligned with [Western liberal democracies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_democracy "Liberal democracy").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-1)

The Olympics’ utility as a crisis-response tool became even more evident with the [1998 Nagano Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Winter_Olympics "1998 Winter Olympics"), held in the shadow of the [Asian Financial Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Asian_financial_crisis "1997 Asian financial crisis"). While neighboring countries like South Korea and Thailand struggled with IMF-imposed austerity, Japan sought to distinguish itself as a stable economic force capable of weathering regional turmoil.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:0-2) The Nagano Olympics not only aimed to boost tourism and consumer confidence but also featured performances by Western orchestras and artists, symbolizing Japan's cultural connectivity and shared values with the West.

The decision to pursue the [2020 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics")—despite the enormous public cost and eventual delay due to [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19")—reflected similar motivations. Government officials emphasized the Games as a necessary stimulus for Japan's sluggish economy and an opportunity to showcase its technological sophistication and preparedness in crisis.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:0-2)

Japan won its first medals in [1920](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_1920_Summer_Olympics "Japan at the 1920 Summer Olympics"), and its first gold medals in [1928](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_1928_Summer_Olympics "Japan at the 1928 Summer Olympics"). Japanese athletes have won 542 medals at the [Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games") (except [art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1936 Summer Olympics")), with the most gold medals won in [judo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judo_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Judo at the Summer Olympics"), [gymnastics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnastics_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Gymnastics at the Summer Olympics"), [wrestling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrestling_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Wrestling at the Summer Olympics"), and [swimming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Swimming at the Summer Olympics"), as of the end of the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics"). Japan has also won 76 medals at the [Winter Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Olympic_Games "Winter Olympic Games"). Its most successful Olympics is the [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") Games hosted in Tokyo.

The [Japanese Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Olympic_Committee "Japanese Olympic Committee") was created in 1911 and recognized in 1912.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-3)

## Medals in art competitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Medals in art competitions")]

Main article: [List of Olympic medalists in art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_medalists_in_art_competitions "List of Olympic medalists in art competitions")

In addition to its accomplishments in sport, Japan has also earned recognition in Olympic [art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the Summer Olympics")—one of the three [non-sports events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_sports#Feats_and_artistic_events "Olympic sports") once included in the Olympic Games. The country won a total of two art competition medals (2 bronze), both at the [1936 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1936 Summer Olympics").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-olympics_jpn-6) These events were part of the official Olympic program in seven Summer Games, from 1912 to 1948. In 1952, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) formally discontinued all non-sport events (including art competitions), as well as awards for feats (such as [alpinism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpinism_at_the_Olympic_Games "Alpinism at the Olympic Games") and [aeronautics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautics_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics "Aeronautics at the 1936 Summer Olympics")). These were subsequently removed from official national medal counts.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-e048-8)[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-art-7)

## Hosted Olympics mottos

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Hosted Olympics mottos")]

### 1964 Summer Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 1964 Summer Olympics")]

The [1964 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Summer_Olympics "1964 Summer Olympics") marks Japan hosting its first Olympic Games. It was held in the capital [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo"). It was also the first time it was held in Asia.

### 1972 Winter Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: 1972 Winter Olympics")]

The [1972 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Winter_Olympics "1972 Winter Olympics") marks the second time Olympics held in Japan. They were held in [Sapporo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapporo "Sapporo").

Because of its snowy geographic, Japan would hosts its first Winter Olympics. It was also the first [winter olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Olympics "Winter Olympics") held in Asia.

### 1998 Winter Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: 1998 Winter Olympics")]

The [1998 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Winter_Olympics "1998 Winter Olympics") was the third time Japan hosted the Olympics and second for Winter. Was held at [Nagano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagano_(city) "Nagano (city)"). The motto of the games is _Coexistence with Nature_ (自然との共存)

### 2020 Summer Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: 2020 Summer Olympics")]

The [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") marks the fourth time the Olympics was held in Japan. It was the first time it was held one year late (2021 instead of 2020) following the worldwide [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"). It marks the second time it was held in Tokyo. Its motto was _United by Emotion_ (感動で、私たちはひとつになる). During that time, only the English version was used.

This motto appeals that "Sports enable us to overcome different environments and become one world through emotions such as joy and excitement that the athletes' competitive performances bring together in our hearts."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-11)

[Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") first participated at the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") in 1912, and has competed at almost every Games since then. The nation was not invited to the 1948 Games after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), and was part of the [American-led boycott of the 1980 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American-led_boycott_of_the_1980_Summer_Olympics "American-led boycott of the 1980 Summer Olympics") in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow").

Since its first (ultimately canceled) bid in 1940, Japan has hosted the Olympics four times: in 1964, 1972, 1998, and 2021 (originally 2020). Each occasion coincided with critical turning points in Japan's domestic development or global standing. The [1964 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Summer_Olympics "1964 Summer Olympics") were a pivotal moment in Japan's postwar recovery, offering a visual spectacle of modernization that included the unveiling of the [Shinkansen bullet train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinkansen "Shinkansen") and the rapid reconstruction of Tokyo's infrastructure. The event symbolized Japan's reintegration into the international community after its defeat in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_in_WWII "Japan in WWII"), marking its transition from a militaristic empire to a peaceful economic power aligned with [Western liberal democracies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_democracy "Liberal democracy").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-1)

The Olympics’ utility as a crisis-response tool became even more evident with the [1998 Nagano Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Winter_Olympics "1998 Winter Olympics"), held in the shadow of the [Asian Financial Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Asian_financial_crisis "1997 Asian financial crisis"). While neighboring countries like South Korea and Thailand struggled with IMF-imposed austerity, Japan sought to distinguish itself as a stable economic force capable of weathering regional turmoil.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:0-2) The Nagano Olympics not only aimed to boost tourism and consumer confidence but also featured performances by Western orchestras and artists, symbolizing Japan's cultural connectivity and shared values with the West.

The decision to pursue the [2020 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics")—despite the enormous public cost and eventual delay due to [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19")—reflected similar motivations. Government officials emphasized the Games as a necessary stimulus for Japan's sluggish economy and an opportunity to showcase its technological sophistication and preparedness in crisis.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:0-2)

Japan won its first medals in [1920](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_1920_Summer_Olympics "Japan at the 1920 Summer Olympics"), and its first gold medals in [1928](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_1928_Summer_Olympics "Japan at the 1928 Summer Olympics"). Japanese athletes have won 542 medals at the [Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games") (except [art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1936 Summer Olympics")), with the most gold medals won in [judo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judo_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Judo at the Summer Olympics"), [gymnastics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnastics_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Gymnastics at the Summer Olympics"), [wrestling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrestling_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Wrestling at the Summer Olympics"), and [swimming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Swimming at the Summer Olympics"), as of the end of the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics"). Japan has also won 76 medals at the [Winter Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Olympic_Games "Winter Olympic Games"). Its most successful Olympics is the [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") Games hosted in Tokyo.

The [Japanese Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Olympic_Committee "Japanese Olympic Committee") was created in 1911 and recognized in 1912.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-3)

## Medals in art competitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Medals in art competitions")]

Main article: [List of Olympic medalists in art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_medalists_in_art_competitions "List of Olympic medalists in art competitions")

In addition to its accomplishments in sport, Japan has also earned recognition in Olympic [art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the Summer Olympics")—one of the three [non-sports events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_sports#Feats_and_artistic_events "Olympic sports") once included in the Olympic Games. The country won a total of two art competition medals (2 bronze), both at the [1936 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1936 Summer Olympics").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-olympics_jpn-6) These events were part of the official Olympic program in seven Summer Games, from 1912 to 1948. In 1952, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) formally discontinued all non-sport events (including art competitions), as well as awards for feats (such as [alpinism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpinism_at_the_Olympic_Games "Alpinism at the Olympic Games") and [aeronautics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautics_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics "Aeronautics at the 1936 Summer Olympics")). These were subsequently removed from official national medal counts.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-e048-8)[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-art-7)

## Hosted Olympics mottos

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Hosted Olympics mottos")]

### 1964 Summer Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 1964 Summer Olympics")]

The [1964 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Summer_Olympics "1964 Summer Olympics") marks Japan hosting its first Olympic Games. It was held in the capital [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo"). It was also the first time it was held in Asia.

### 1972 Winter Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: 1972 Winter Olympics")]

The [1972 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Winter_Olympics "1972 Winter Olympics") marks the second time Olympics held in Japan. They were held in [Sapporo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapporo "Sapporo").

Because of its snowy geographic, Japan would hosts its first Winter Olympics. It was also the first [winter olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Olympics "Winter Olympics") held in Asia.

### 1998 Winter Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: 1998 Winter Olympics")]

The [1998 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Winter_Olympics "1998 Winter Olympics") was the third time Japan hosted the Olympics and second for Winter. Was held at [Nagano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagano_(city) "Nagano (city)"). The motto of the games is _Coexistence with Nature_ (自然との共存)

### 2020 Summer Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: 2020 Summer Olympics")]

The [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") marks the fourth time the Olympics was held in Japan. It was the first time it was held one year late (2021 instead of 2020) following the worldwide [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"). It marks the second time it was held in Tokyo. Its motto was _United by Emotion_ (感動で、私たちはひとつになる). During that time, only the English version was used.

This motto appeals that "Sports enable us to overcome different environments and become one world through emotions such as joy and excitement that the athletes' competitive performances bring together in our hearts."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-11)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about the team organized by the People's Republic of China to compete in the Olympics. For the team organized by the Republic of China to compete in the Olympics from 1924 to 1948, see [Republic of China at the Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_at_the_Olympics "Republic of China at the Olympics"). For the team now representing the Republic of China on Taiwan, see [Chinese Taipei at the Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Taipei_at_the_Olympics "Chinese Taipei at the Olympics"). For the Olympics in China, see [Chinese Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Olympics_(disambiguation) "Chinese Olympics (disambiguation)").

The [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") (commonly known as China)'s participation in the Olympic games is relatively recent. Largely due to the [Cultural Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution") and the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee")'s recognition of the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China "Republic of China"), The People's Republic of China did not participate in the Olympics for over 20 years; recognition of the [Chinese Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Olympic_Committee "Chinese Olympic Committee")—or CHN—did not happen until 1979. The People's Republic of China sent its first full athletic delegation to the [Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games") in the [1984 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics") which was held in Los Angeles, United States.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-1984_olympics-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:1-2)

As of 2026, China has finished at 1st place in the Summer Olympics once, at 2nd place four times, and 3rd place twice. It has won a total of 330 gold medals, 262 silver medals and 227 bronze medals over the course of 13 Olympic games.

With the nation's 12th appearance at the Summer and 13th appearance at the Winter Olympics, China is the most successful country overall in the [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia")–[Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania "Oceania") region, making them the [3rd most successful country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-time_Olympic_Games_medal_table#Complete_ranked_medals_(excluding_precursors) "All-time Olympic Games medal table") in Olympic history, after the United States and the Soviet Union.

## Participation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Participation")]

Originally having participated in Olympics as the delegation of the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_at_the_Olympics "Republic of China at the Olympics") (ROC) from [1924](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1924_Summer_Olympics "1924 Summer Olympics") to [1948](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_at_the_1948_Summer_Olympics "Republic of China at the 1948 Summer Olympics"), China competed at the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") under the name of the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") (PRC) for the first time at the [1952 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1952_Summer_Olympics "1952 Summer Olympics") held in [Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki "Helsinki"), [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland"), although they only arrived in time during the last days to participate in one event.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-1952_olympics-3) That year, the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") (IOC) allowed both the PRC and ROC (Republic of China) (which fled to Taiwan after the [Chinese Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War")) to compete with the name "China", although the latter withdrew in protest.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-1952_olympics-3) Due to the dispute over the political status of the "two Chinas", the PRC started a period of isolationism, withdrawing from several international sporting bodies and the UN system until the mid-1970s, when the country participated for the first time in the [Asian Games in 1974](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Asian_Games "1974 Asian Games") and the [World University Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_University_Games "World University Games") in 1977. Returning to the IOC officially only in 1979, which gave it the right to send an official delegation, starting from the [1980 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Winter_Olympics "1980 Winter Olympics") in [Lake Placid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Placid,_New_York "Lake Placid, New York"), [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-1952_olympics-3) Their first appearance at the [Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games") after 1952 was the [1984 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics") in Los Angeles, United States.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-1984_olympics-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:1-2)

## Designation Issues - PRC versus ROC and classification of Hong Kong

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Designation Issues - PRC versus ROC and classification of Hong Kong")]

The [Chinese Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Olympic_Committee "Chinese Olympic Committee") in its current form was recognized in 1979.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-1952_olympics-3) Before the [Chinese Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War"), athletes competed as the Republic of China (ROC) at the Olympics. The ROC continued to compete from 1952 (Summer Olympics) to 1976 (Winter Olympics), but only representing athletes from the island of Taiwan (although the football team members of ROC in the [1960 Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_Summer_Olympic_Games "1960 Summer Olympic Games") were overseas Hong Kongers). The [dispute over use of the name _China_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_the_United_Nations "China and the United Nations") resulted in the PRC boycotting the Games completely during these years. In 1979, the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") approved the [Nagoya Resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_at_the_Olympics#Nagoya_Resolution "Republic of China at the Olympics") in which the name "China" would be owned by the National Olympic Committee of the People's Republic of China, based in Beijing. While the Republic of China headquartered in Taipei would be called as _[Chinese Taipei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese\_Taipei\_at\_the\_Olympics "Chinese Taipei at the Olympics")_, which also regulated the use of national symbols during the Games and any related events; this reopened the door for the PRC to finally join the Olympic movement.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-1952_olympics-3)

[Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_at_the_Olympics "Hong Kong at the Olympics") has had a distinct [National Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Olympic_Committee "National Olympic Committee") since 1950 and has competed at the Games since 1952.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-HK-4) After the territory was returned to the PRC and the Hong Kong [Special Administrative Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Administrative_Region_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China") was created in 1997, this arrangement has continued, with Hong Kong competing independently from the rest of the nation under the name _[Hong Kong, China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Federation\_and\_Olympic\_Committee\_of\_Hong\_Kong,\_China "Sports Federation and Olympic Committee of Hong Kong, China")_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-HK-4) China is ranked fourth by total number of medals in the Olympic Games.

## Olympic bids and hosted Games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Olympic bids and hosted Games")]

The People's Republic of China has hosted the Games on two occasions: in [2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") and in [2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Winter_Olympics "2022 Winter Olympics"). [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing") is the first city to have hosted both the Summer and Winter Olympics.

### 2008 Summer Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2008 Summer Olympics")]

Following [economic reforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_and_opening_up "Reform and opening up") under [Deng Xiaoping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping "Deng Xiaoping"), China underwent rapid economic growth. As a result, China successfully bid in 2001 to host the 2008 Olympic Games, signaling the [CHN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Olympic_Committee "Chinese Olympic Committee")'s debut as an Olympic host.

In order to host the 2008 Olympics Games, significant investment—particularly from the [Government of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China")—was necessary. With contributions from both the public and private sectors, the central government allocated an estimated ¥313 billion [CNY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renminbi "Renminbi") ($6.8 billion USD) to the Games. Associated expenses of hosting, such as infrastructure and developmental costs brought the total investment to around ¥313 billion CNY (roughly $43 billion USD), making it the biggest investment in an Olympics game yet. The event alone generated a profit of over ¥1 billion CNY.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:2-5)

The 2008 Olympic Games helped China reshape its international image by utilizing the country’s rich historical culture to divert attention from its past. The Olympics [Fuwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuwa "Fuwa") mascots were designed to be deeply embedded in Chinese culture, with each ring associated with an aspect of Chinese heritage. Not only was the event able to bring a wider range of China’s culture to a global audience, China’s decision to represent one of the mascots, namely Yingying, as a [Tibetan antelope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_antelope "Tibetan antelope") was an attempt to legitimize its [annexation of Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annexation_of_Tibet_by_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Annexation of Tibet by the People's Republic of China") through symbolic entrenchment—a diplomatic practice used to justify the [CCP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party")'s regional occupation through military incursion in 1951.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:3-6)

Such extensive state involvement[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:5-7) indicated the state's goal as presenting China as an emerging global power.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:4-8) Preparation for the Games created millions of jobs for the domestic economy and bolstered nationalism significantly, while successfully hosting the event boosted tourism and increased foreign investments and confidence. Consequently, the country saw a GDP growth of 9.7% in the next year despite the effects of the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis").

### Early appearance and hiatus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Early appearance and hiatus")]

After the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949, PRC sent a delegation to the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") for the first time at the [1952 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1952_Summer_Olympics "1952 Summer Olympics") in Helsinki, Finland. The Chinese delegation (including athletes and officials) consisted of 38 men and 2 women,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-China_Olympism-12) including the [men's football team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_national_football_team "China national football team"), the [men's basketball team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_men's_national_basketball_team "China men's national basketball team"), and one swimmer. Only the swimmer arrived in time to take part in the official competition, and the football team played two friendly matches.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:3-6) The Chinese stayed ten days in Helsinki and participated in the closing ceremony. The Republic of China's (ROC) team withdrew from the Games on July 17 in response to the [IOC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee")'s decision to allow both PRC and ROC sportsmen and women to compete.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:4-8) This marked the beginning of the "two Chinas" conflict in the Olympic Movement, which resulted in the [Chinese Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Olympic_Committee "Chinese Olympic Committee")'s withdrawal from the IOC in August 1958.

In the 1970s, China normalized her relations with the United States through [Ping Pong Diplomacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ping_Pong_Diplomacy "Ping Pong Diplomacy"), and established diplomatic relations with the United States on January 1, 1979. The normalization finally led to the [Chinese Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Olympic_Committee "Chinese Olympic Committee")'s return to the IOC on October 25, 1979.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-China_Olympism-12)

China boycotted the [1980 Olympic games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics "1980 Summer Olympics") in Moscow.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:02-13):161

#### Sports summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Sports summary")]

Till 2012, China won three-quarters of their gold medals (152 out of 201) and two-thirds of their medals (311 out of 473) in six sports: [table tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_tennis_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Table tennis at the Summer Olympics"), [badminton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badminton_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Badminton at the Summer Olympics"), [diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Diving at the Summer Olympics"), [gymnastics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnastics_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Gymnastics at the Summer Olympics"), [weightlifting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weightlifting_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Weightlifting at the Summer Olympics"), and [shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shooting_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Shooting at the Summer Olympics").

China recently dominated the gold medals in table tennis, badminton and diving. China won all golds four times in table tennis and one time in badminton, and won three-quarters of all diving golds since 1992.

The total dominance in table tennis and badminton has also lead to negative consequences. Due to the low participations among non-Asian countries, these two sports may lose their positions in the Summer Olympics just like **baseball** and **softball** did after 2008.

While through the years, Chinese athletes have made significant progress in sports in which China was less dominant. Among them, swimming is the potential one that may get into top five sports of China in the near future.

#### 1984

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: 1984")]

China won 15 golds and ranked 4th at the [1984 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics") in Los Angeles.

**[Xu Haifeng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xu_Haifeng "Xu Haifeng")** won the first-ever gold medal for China in the shooting event of _50 m Pistol_. It was called "a break through zero" – an event that brought great joy to the whole Chinese nation.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-1984_olympics-1)

[Li Ning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Ning "Li Ning") won six medals in gymnastics, 3 golds, 2 silvers, and 1 bronze, earning him the nickname "Prince of Gymnasts" in China.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:2-5) Six medals in a single Olympics is still the record for any Chinese athlete.

Chinese women's volleyball team defeated USA women's team in the final and won China's first ball-game gold medal.

#### 1988

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: 1988")]

China won 5 golds and ranked 11th at the [1988 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Summer_Olympics "1988 Summer Olympics") at Seoul, South Korea.

[Li Meisu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Meisu "Li Meisu") won China's first medal in athletics.

China also won first medals in rowing. A silver in _women's coxed fours_ and a bronze in _women's eights_

#### 1992

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=China_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: 1992")]

China won 16 golds and ranked 4th at the [1992 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Summer_Olympics "1992 Summer Olympics") at Barcelona, Spain.

[Chen Yueling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chen_Yueling "Chen Yueling") won China's first athletics gold medal in _women's 10 km walk_.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about the team organized by the People's Republic of China to compete in the Olympics. For the team organized by the Republic of China to compete in the Olympics from 1924 to 1948, see [Republic of China at the Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_at_the_Olympics "Republic of China at the Olympics"). For the team now representing the Republic of China on Taiwan, see [Chinese Taipei at the Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Taipei_at_the_Olympics "Chinese Taipei at the Olympics"). For the Olympics in China, see [Chinese Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Olympics_(disambiguation) "Chinese Olympics (disambiguation)").
